luxury-china-green-shoots.headline: Europe's luxury giants spot 'green shoots' in China demand
luxury-china-green-shoots.body_md:
The Chinese shopper who spent much of the past eighteen months trimming spend on handbags, watches and cosmetics is showing tentative signs of coming back — and Europe's luxury houses, which have spent that stretch bracing for worse, are starting to say so out loud.

![The Louis, Louis Vuitton's ship-shaped flagship store in Shanghai](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/92/The_Louis%2C_Louis_Vuitton_Flagship_Store_20251128.jpg)

LVMH, Hermès and Kering all pointed to improving Chinese trends in their most recent results, according to a Bloomberg report this week, with executives and analysts converging on similar language: not a recovery, but the first believable signs one might be coming.

## What the numbers actually show

LVMH's fashion and leather goods division — the group's largest and the one most exposed to discretionary Chinese spending — returned to 1% organic growth in the second quarter, reversing a 2% decline in the first. Group-wide, Asia excluding Japan grew 6% on a like-for-like basis in the first half, though the pace slowed from 7% in the first quarter to roughly 4% in the second, a reminder that the improvement is uneven rather than a straight line up. TD Cowen analyst Oliver Chen described China as "stabilizing after several quarters of deterioration."

Hermès, which has weathered the downturn better than most rivals thanks to its waiting-list model for handbags, grew revenue 6.1% at constant exchange rates in the first half to €8.16 billion. Its Asia-Pacific division excluding Japan grew a more modest 2.4% at constant rates, with management citing "continued growth in Greater China" while adding they were "seeing the Chinese market stabilising, but not yet seeing a decisive turnaround." The company has kept investing regardless, opening a store in Beijing's Sanlitun district this year and expanding its Hong Kong and Taipei locations.

Kering, the group hit hardest by the slowdown as it works through a rebuilding of Gucci, posted its first positive quarterly result in the region in two years. Chief executive Luca de Meo has called China a "top strategic priority," and the company is now expected to return to regional sales growth by the fourth quarter. Richemont, owner of Cartier, has leaned on a comeback in Hong Kong and Macau tourism rather than mainland spending directly. Burberry, smaller than the others but a useful bellwether, reported a 9% jump in Greater China retail sales last quarter, which it attributed partly to demand from younger, Gen Z shoppers.

## The catch

The recovery, such as it is, remains lopsided and fragile. Sales at the twenty-five largest luxury labels operating in China fell more than 10% in July, as Beijing's efforts to curb capital outflows and tax offshore wealth continued to dent spending among the country's wealthiest citizens — precisely the cohort that drives high-ticket purchases. What growth exists looks distinctly K-shaped: high-net-worth consumers and categories like premium cosmetics are recovering faster than the broader middle-class spender who powered the sector's boom years through the late 2010s. Deutsche Bank's Do-Hyun Yoo put it plainly: without a genuine improvement in Chinese consumer confidence, "the path to reacceleration remains uncertain."

That caveat matters for how the numbers should be read. China accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of global luxury spending once tourist purchases are included, so even a modest change in trajectory moves group-level results for LVMH, Kering and Hermès more than almost anything else in their business. It is also why LVMH shares are still down around 30% for the year despite the improving second-quarter print — investors had already been burned once by premature optimism about a China rebound, most recently when hopes for a post-pandemic snapback faded through 2023 and 2024.

## What's next

The next real test comes with third-quarter trading updates in October, which will show whether the sequential improvement seen through the summer survives the government's continued crackdown on capital flight — the single biggest swing factor for the segment of shoppers actually driving the numbers. Kering's promised return to regional growth in the fourth quarter is the most concrete marker on the calendar; a miss there would undercut the broader stabilization narrative fastest.

ofcom-sky-news-farage-probe.headline: Ofcom opens formal probe into Sky News over Farage 'harassment' complaint
ofcom-sky-news-farage-probe.body_md:
Ofcom, the UK's broadcasting regulator, has opened a formal investigation into Sky News after Reform UK complained that a reporter's visit to Nigel Farage's daughter's home breached rules on privacy, accuracy and impartiality. The inquiry, confirmed on 20 August, turns on an episode from 6 July that has become a proxy fight over how far political scrutiny can reach into a public figure's family life — and over how readily broadcasting regulation can be summoned as a weapon in that fight.

The facts, as both sides broadly agree on them: a Sky News reporter went to a property linked to Farage's daughter while the Reform UK leader was out of the country, seeking comment on a story about donations he had received from George Cottrell, a longtime associate who served eight months in a US prison in 2017 after pleading guilty to wire fraud. Cottrell had paid for a £15,000 flight that took Farage from New Jersey to Palm Beach, Florida, for a widely photographed meeting with Elon Musk, and had covered a £9,000 trip to Belgium; Cottrell's mother, Fiona Cottrell, has given Reform UK £500,000. The Sunday Times had reported the gifts were undeclared.

![Official portrait of Nigel Farage](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Official_portrait_of_Nigel_Farage_MP_crop_2.jpg)

## What happened at the door

Sky News says its account was narrower than Reform UK's version suggests: on a single occasion, it says, a reporter approached the property without a camera operator, identified themselves, and the adult occupant declined to engage. The broadcaster maintains it did not otherwise contact Farage's family over the story. Farage disputes that characterisation. Confronted by a Sky News journalist shortly afterwards, he warned: "You tell your bosses, you harass my family any more and there will be serious consequences. That is what your organisation has done this morning." Reform UK's formal complaint went further, arguing that Sky's coverage of the episode itself misrepresented Farage as dishonest and omitted his daughter's account that she felt "harassed and unsafe" by media attention at her home.

## The regulatory question

Ofcom's broadcasting code allows it to investigate claims of unfair treatment and unwarranted infringement of privacy, and separately covers due impartiality and factual accuracy — and Reform UK's complaint invoked all three strands at once. The regulator can, if it upholds a complaint, direct broadcasters to air a statement of its findings, and in serious or repeated cases fine a licensee or in principle revoke its licence. It cannot compel an on-air apology or correction of the kind Reform UK has demanded, which sits at the more punitive end of what complainants often ask for regardless of what the code allows.

That gap between what is demanded and what Ofcom can actually order is not new, but it matters here because the complaint arrives already dressed as a public campaign rather than a quiet regulatory filing. Farage's Reform UK now polls as Britain's most popular party by some measures, and its relationship with broadcast media — Sky, the BBC, GB News — has become a recurring front in its political strategy, with complaints and public denunciations of coverage serving alongside conventional campaigning.

## Why it matters beyond one doorstep

Ofcom investigations into major broadcasters over privacy and impartiality are not rare, but they are usually triggered by viewer complaints in bulk or by identifiable factual disputes, not by the subject of a story who is also the leader of a political party gaining ground in the polls. A formal probe launched on those terms invites the question of whether regulatory process is being used to contest an editorial decision that a public figure simply disliked. Sky News has not said whether it will alter its reporting practices while the investigation proceeds; Ofcom has not set a timetable for a ruling.

The outcome will be watched less for its narrow verdict on one doorstep encounter than for what it signals about the threshold at which political pressure translates into regulatory scrutiny of newsrooms covering politicians' finances and family.

russia-mobilization-readiness-test.headline: WSJ: Russia quietly tests readiness for fresh mobilization drive
russia-mobilization-readiness-test.body_md:
Russia's armed forces spent part of July running a quiet logistical drill: could the system built to absorb a mass wave of new conscripts actually cope, if the order came? According to *The Wall Street Journal*, exercises in the Kaliningrad region and elsewhere tested the unglamorous machinery of mobilization — receiving, housing, feeding and arming large numbers of men — without any public announcement that a new call-up was imminent.

> Russia's military has been stress testing its ability to absorb a mass of new recruits in case the Kremlin orders a fresh mobilization push for the first time since 2022.

That is the sentence doing the work here. No decision has been made, the Kremlin and Russia's defence ministry both declined to comment on the report, and Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Security Council, has repeatedly dismissed mobilization talk as "nonsense" and a Ukrainian "lying provocation." But testing the plumbing in advance of a decision is itself a signal — the kind of preparatory step militaries take when they want the option available on short notice, not when they've ruled it out.

![Vladimir Putin observes military exercises with Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu during the Vostok-2022 command post exercise.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Putin_at_military_exercises_%282022%29_02.jpg)

## The arithmetic behind the drill

The pressure is coming from the casualty ledger. Ukraine's General Staff put Russian losses at over 42,000 killed, wounded, missing or captured in July alone — a monthly high for 2026 — with the year's average running near 34,000 a month and cumulative losses since January topping 160,000. Voluntary contract recruitment, the mechanism Moscow has leaned on since the unpopular 2022 draft, is no longer keeping pace: for the first time since the invasion began, Russia is reportedly losing troops faster than it is signing them up, even after raising enlistment bonuses.

That gap is what a fresh mobilization would exist to close. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this week that Russian planning points to roughly 300,000 additional troops, deliberately structured as a "peripheral mobilization" that avoids Moscow and St Petersburg to limit political blowback in the two cities most sensitive to public opinion — with a further escalation toward 500,000 floated for 2027. Zelensky offered no public evidence for the figures, and Moscow has not confirmed them, but they track with the WSJ's separate reporting that any new wave would likely draw on Russians with little to no military background, unlike the reservists and veterans mobilized in 2022.

## Why the Duma comes first

The timing tells its own story. State Duma elections run September 18-20, and the Kremlin is not expected to announce anything before votes are counted — a decision that would reintroduce, on the eve of a national poll, the same scenes of queues at border crossings and family send-offs that made the 2022 mobilization one of the more visibly unpopular moments of the war. Medvedev's public denials are consistent with an administration managing the story until the election is safely past, not necessarily with an absence of planning underneath.

Kaliningrad's inclusion in the drills adds a second layer analysts are watching separately from the Ukraine front: the exclave sits between Poland and Lithuania, adjacent to the Suwałki Corridor that would be the flashpoint in any NATO contingency, and testing mobilization logistics there suggests planning horizons that extend beyond the current war's immediate battlefield needs.

The next marker is the Duma vote itself. If the Kremlin follows the pattern its own officials are describing — quiet preparation, public denial, and a decision deferred until the ballots are counted — the period immediately after September 20 is when any formal mobilization order, if one comes, would surface.

offender-exclusion-zones-october.headline: New electronic exclusion-zone scheme for offenders to start in October
offender-exclusion-zones-october.body_md:
From October, some of England and Wales's most serious sexual and violent offenders leaving prison will be confined to GPS-monitored "restriction zones" — areas a few miles wide that they cannot leave without triggering an alert to probation officers. Step outside the boundary, and the consequence can be a trip straight back to prison.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris announced the October start date this month, framing it as a shift in whose life gets constrained after a conviction. "Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he said. "No victim should fear the shadow of an abuser on their back."

![Electronic ankle tag used for GPS monitoring](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/Ankle_monitor_%283767974058%29.jpg)

The scheme is a variation on a familiar idea. Courts already impose exclusion zones — bans on entering a specific street, a victim's workplace, a named postcode. Restriction zones flip the logic: rather than naming places an offender can't go, probation officers and victims jointly agree the (usually larger) area an offender must stay inside, using a GPS ankle tag to enforce it. Officers can set the boundary for as long as they judge necessary and adjust it as risk changes.

## The system doing the enforcing is already under strain

The technical and human infrastructure behind this — enforced by Serco under a roughly £200m, six-year Ministry of Justice contract awarded in 2023 — is the part worth watching. The National Audit Office reported in July that electronic monitoring "is not working as intended," warning of risks to public protection. Serco met its target for turning up to fit tags on time in February, but succeeded in actually fitting one within two attempts only 62% of the time. HM Prison and Probation Service was, as of March, reviewing roughly 8,900 cases — nearly a quarter of everyone required to be tagged — to work out how many people were going unmonitored. Probation itself is short an estimated 2,200 staff.

The NAO's conclusion was blunt: further expansion won't be safe or effective unless the Ministry of Justice and its partners fix governance, data quality and system-wide inefficiencies first. The government's response is to throw money and headcount at the problem — up to £700m in extra probation funding by 2028-29, and more than 1,300 new trainee probation officers due to start this year — rather than to slow the rollout.

For a technology story, the interesting gap is what's still missing: no vendor beyond Serco has been named for the restriction-zone software layer itself, and the Ministry of Justice has not published a breakdown of what the October expansion will cost beyond the existing tagging contract. Serco is listed on the London Stock Exchange, making it the one publicly traded company with a direct, quantifiable stake in how smoothly this scales. Whether "tens of thousands more offenders tagged," as ministers have promised, is achievable on the current contract — or requires a new one — should become clear once the scheme is live and the NAO, or MPs on the Public Accounts Committee, take another look.

esports-research-scheme.headline: Students paid up to £2,000 to play video games in new esports research scheme
esports-research-scheme.body_md:
It sounds like the pitch of a bored teenager: get paid to play video games. But the actual offer, from the University of Roehampton in south-west London, is more measured than the headline suggests — a £2,000-a-year scholarship for students who can prove they are genuinely good at competitive gaming, not a stipend for anyone willing to sit down with a controller.

Roehampton launched the scheme in 2018, the first UK university to do so, and has now handed out more than 100 of the awards. Up to 20 scholarships go out each year, plus four reserved under a Women in Esports scheme — Europe's first — aimed at a competitive scene still dominated by men. Recipients must hit minimum in-game rankings (Diamond tier in League of Legends, for instance), compete in weekly university tournaments, represent Roehampton at live events, and keep up their coursework. It is closer to a sports scholarship than a research grant: the money buys competitive commitment, not lab time.

> "This money was crucial to me as it gave me the opportunity to study in a very expensive city without needing part-time work," said Cameron Dray, a former Roehampton esports scholar.

![University of Roehampton's Whitelands College, one of the constituent colleges running the esports scholarship scheme](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/dc/University_of_Roehampton%2C_Whitelands_College.jpg)

## Academia catches up

What has changed since 2018 is the company Roehampton now keeps. In February, Loughborough University — a heavyweight in sports science — signed a memorandum of understanding with the British Esports Federation and opened a 40-machine Esports Gaming Lab as part of its DigiLabs campus, with an explicit remit to research performance, coaching and safeguarding standards across the sector. Staffordshire University has run the UK's first esports degree since 2017. None of this amounts to a single coordinated "research scheme" — it is several universities independently deciding esports is worth institutional attention, nearly a decade after Roehampton made the first move.

That lag is the real story. Ukie, the UK games trade body, valued the domestic esports sector's economic contribution at £111.5m in gross value added and over 1,200 jobs as far back as 2020; broader UK esports and gaming market estimates now run into the billions, with double-digit annual growth. Venture capital, publishers and sponsors priced in esports' commercial potential years before a psychology department did. Universities are not spotting an opportunity here so much as formalising one that already has a stock price.

## Why the money still matters

For students, the practical case is straightforward: London is expensive, and £2,000 covers a meaningful chunk of living costs for someone already spending 20-plus hours a week on ranked play. For the sector, scholarships and lab partnerships do a quieter job — they signal to parents, employers and government bodies that competitive gaming is a legitimate field of study rather than a hobby with a degree bolted on, a stigma esports courses have fought since Staffordshire's launch drew tabloid mockery in 2017.

What is genuinely new, and worth watching, is the shift from scholarship money — paying good players to keep playing — toward research infrastructure like Loughborough's lab, which exists to study players rather than simply fund them. That is a different kind of institutional bet, and one still in its early innings.

The next marker is whether Loughborough's lab produces published findings, and whether other Russell Group universities follow with dedicated esports research funding rather than scholarship schemes alone. Until then, the money on offer is real, but it is paying for talent, not answering questions about what gaming does to the people — or the economy — around it.

europe-ac-emissions-survey.headline: Europeans favour air conditioning over emissions cuts as heatwaves intensify
europe-ac-emissions-survey.body_md:
Four heatwaves have swept across Europe this year, several pushing temperatures close to or above 40C, and a new poll suggests the public has reached a verdict on what should happen next: install more air conditioning, climate arithmetic notwithstanding.

YouGov surveyed adults in France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Spain in mid-July, and in the UK in early August. Across all six countries, between 61% and 73% said air conditioning should be installed as standard in new homes. A further 65% to 75% backed making it easier to fit AC without needing permission from a council or landlord, and 52% to 66% supported government subsidies to help pay for it.

![Air conditioning units mounted on a building facade](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/45/Air_conditioners_in_Nis.jpg)

Set against that is a trade-off most respondents resolved without much hesitation. In every country except Italy, 41% to 48% said encouraging more air conditioning to reduce heatwave harm should be prioritised over cutting CO2 emissions, against just 20% to 33% who put emissions first. Cooling a home mechanically is estimated to account for roughly 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions — on some estimates, close to double the aviation industry's share — a fact that appears to weigh little against the immediate discomfort, and danger, of extreme heat. More people across the six countries thought expanding air conditioning would meaningfully cut heatwave harm (29% to 61%) than thought it would meaningfully move their country's climate figures (19% to 40%).

## Britain lags, but wants in

The starkest divide in the poll is not about attitudes but about access. Current air conditioning take-up stands at 63% in Italy and 58% in Spain, against 30% in France, 23% in Poland, 16% in Germany and just 11% in the UK — the lowest of the six, and consistent with separate estimates that put British household AC ownership in the low single digits a few years ago. Cost was cited by 51% to 75% of respondents as the main barrier to owning a unit, far outweighing climate concerns, which only 27% of French respondents named as a factor.

The gap matters because it tracks with outcomes. Between 79% and 85% of people with air conditioning said they kept their homes comfortable during recent heatwaves, compared with just 35% to 47% of those without it. Between 30% and 52% said they had feared for a household member's health at or near 40C — fear that appears to be driving the appetite for mandates even in countries, like the UK, where the building stock and planning system have historically resisted cooling infrastructure.

The policy question now sits with Brussels. The European Commission's Electrification Action Plan, published in July, nudged the bloc toward heat pumps and efficient cooling, but the companion Heating and Cooling Strategy — meant to set the terms for how the EU squares rising cooling demand with its emissions targets — has slipped to the third quarter of 2026. Until it lands, national governments are left to referee the same trade-off the public has already settled in its own favour: comfort now, emissions later.

astrazeneca-80bn-pipeline.headline: AstraZeneca's pipeline momentum fuels $80bn 2030 revenue ambition
astrazeneca-80bn-pipeline.body_md:
AstraZeneca wants to nearly double its annual revenue within four years, and it wants investors to believe the plan is not a bet but an arithmetic exercise. The company's first-half 2026 results, published on 27 July, gave that claim its best evidence yet — and, three weeks earlier, its most public dent.[^1][^2]

Total revenue for the half rose 9% at actual exchange rates to $30.7bn, with core earnings per share up 12% to $5.21. Oncology, the company's largest division, grew 16% at constant exchange rates to $14.1bn — 46% of group revenue — offsetting the loss of US exclusivity on the diabetes drug Farxiga and continued procurement pressure in China. Second-quarter core EPS came in at $2.63, ahead of analyst consensus around $2.48.[^2][^3]

![AstraZeneca's Discovery Centre headquarters and R&D campus in Cambridge, UK](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/AstraZeneca_HQ_in_Cambridge_UK.jpg)

The headline ambition, set out at a 2024 investor day and reaffirmed every quarter since, is $80bn in total revenue by 2030 — roughly double the $45.8bn AstraZeneca reported for 2024 — built on an expected 20 new medicine launches and sustained growth beyond the decade. Chief executive Pascal Soriot has taken to describing the company as moving through a “catalyst-rich period,” a phrase that is, on the evidence of this year, entirely literal.[^1][^4]

## A pipeline built to be counted

AstraZeneca now runs more than 100 Phase III programmes, with management flagging over 20 late-stage readouts due in 2026 alone and 25 across an 18-month window. Six delivered positive results in the first half, including first pivotal data for tozorakimab in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and efzimfotase alfa in hypophosphatasia, alongside continued expansion of the cancer drug Enhertu into earlier-stage disease. The company has also filed or won 30 regulatory approvals across markets since its last annual report.[^1][^2]

Oncology dealmaking has kept pace. In June, AstraZeneca licensed global rights to Zegfrovy (sunvozertinib), an EGFR-inhibitor lung cancer therapy from China's Dizal Pharmaceutical already approved in the US and China, in a deal worth up to $1.5bn — $600m upfront, the rest tied to milestones. The drug treats non-small-cell lung cancer with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations after chemotherapy has failed, a narrow but underserved population where AstraZeneca already has a commercial footprint through Tagrisso. Management has been explicit that the 2030 target does not depend on further acquisitions of this kind — it is meant to be organic, which is precisely why the trial calendar matters so much.[^5]

## The number the plan can't survive without

Here the caution has to be stated plainly, because the underlying statistic is contested. Older industry estimates, often cited in pharma commentary, put Phase III success at roughly 25–30%. More recent analysis covering 2014–2023 puts the figure closer to 50–55% overall, with large-molecule biologics succeeding at higher rates (around 74%) than small molecules (around 61%). Which figure applies to any one AstraZeneca readout depends on modality, disease area and how many prior trials in the same class have already reported — a coin AstraZeneca cannot flip in its favour by force of ambition alone.[^6]

That abstraction became concrete on 9 July, when Wainua (eplontersen), developed with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, missed the primary endpoint of its Phase III CARDIO-TTRansform trial in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy — a composite of cardiovascular death and recurrent cardiovascular events through week 140. The drug had shown positive earlier-stage signals and was not on most analysts' list of high-risk readouts, which was part of the problem: AstraZeneca shares fell more than 9% that day, their worst single session since March 2020, wiping roughly £19bn off market value. A prespecified subgroup on Wainua monotherapy, without background stabiliser drugs, did show a nominally significant benefit, offering a narrower path forward, but the headline result stood.[^7][^8]

> "If three trials fail in a sequence, the widely held view of Astra's market-leading R&D platform might lose its shine."

That warning, attributed to an analyst reviewing the Wainua result, captures the asymmetry investors are now pricing. Jefferies analysts said the single failure did not by itself threaten the $80bn target, but that it could cost the company's R&D credibility — the intangible premium built up over a decade of unusually consistent trial execution. Several noted that the market reaction, a roughly 9–10% share drop, was two to four times larger than most models' estimate of Wainua's standalone contribution to valuation, suggesting the sell-off was as much about doubt in the pipeline's remaining 20-odd readouts as about the one drug that failed.[^7][^8]

## What the arithmetic requires

AstraZeneca's 2026 guidance — mid-to-high single-digit revenue growth and low-double-digit core EPS growth at constant exchange rates — is unaffected by any single readout and remains, for now, intact. The company reiterated the $80bn ambition again at the H1 results, three weeks after Wainua, treating the setback as a data point rather than a reversal.[^1][^2]

But the compounding math behind $80bn assumes a pipeline hit rate meaningfully above what raw Phase III base rates would predict for a portfolio this size — 20-plus readouts is enough volume that ordinary probability, at even the more favourable 50–55% success estimates, implies several more failures are likely before 2030, not merely possible. The company's own framing — that the ambition is “risk-adjusted” — is a tacit admission that management has already built some of that attrition into the forecast. Whether it has built in enough is the question the next 18 months of trial data will answer, one readout at a time.

## What's next

AstraZeneca's third-quarter results, expected in late October, will be the next scheduled checkpoint, alongside further Phase III readouts management has flagged for the second half — most immediately in oncology and respiratory disease, where the company's growth engine is most concentrated. Investors will be watching less for any single trial than for whether Wainua turns out to be an isolated miss or the first of a run; Kumar's three-in-a-row threshold, however informal, is likely to become the market's working test of whether AstraZeneca's R&D premium survives intact.

clark-bmw-championship-win.headline: Wyndham Clark holds off Rory McIlroy fightback to win BMW Championship
clark-bmw-championship-win.body_md:
Wyndham Clark had built a five-shot cushion by the turn at Bellerive Country Club. By the time he stood on the 16th tee, it was gone.

Clark went two-over for his first seven holes on Sunday, missing putts he'd been making all week, while Rory McIlroy reeled off birdies at 8, 9 and 11 to draw level. For a stretch on the back nine, the BMW Championship — the second leg of the PGA Tour's FedExCup playoffs — looked like it might slip away from the 32-year-old entirely.

It didn't. Clark answered with a 232-yard 5-iron to 15 feet at the par-3 16th and made the putt, then birdied the par-5 17th as McIlroy found bunkers and made bogey. A third straight birdie at 18 sealed it: Clark closed with an even-par 70 to finish at 17-under 263, three clear of Patrick Cantlay, with McIlroy third at 13-under.

> "I wasn't really nervous. I was kind of like ... out of it. I was making dumb bogeys," Clark said afterward.

## A messy final round, a clean finish

Cantlay made his own run, five birdies in his first ten holes pulling him into contention, before a double bogey at the 11th — his ball found the water — took the wind out of it. He rallied again, birdieing his final three holes to secure outright second. McIlroy's chance effectively ended at 17, where a wayward drive led to bogey just as Clark birdied the same hole from the group ahead.

It was the kind of final round that made for restless watching rather than a coronation: a five-shot lead reduced to nothing by the turn, then rebuilt in three holes. Clark's own read on it was blunt rather than triumphant.

"Three wins in one season is my best year yet — coming off my worst year ever," he said, a nod to a 2025 campaign that never got going after his breakthrough 2023 U.S. Open title.

![Wyndham Clark](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Wyndham_Clark_2023_01.png)

## Third win, and a case for player of the year

The victory is Clark's third of the 2026 PGA Tour season, a rare clustering that puts him into the player-of-the-year conversation alongside Scottie Scheffler, given that one of the three came at a major and this one at a FedExCup playoff event carrying a $20 million purse. Clark took home $3.6 million of it.

For McIlroy, third place extends a familiar pattern this season: contending deep into Sundays without adding to his win tally. "I always felt like I needed to just get my nose ahead to really try to put the pressure on Wyndham, and I couldn't,” he said.

Further down the leaderboard, the result carried its own consequences. Cantlay's runner-up finish vaulted him from 43rd into the top 30 of the FedExCup standings, as did a strong week from Gary Woodland. Rickie Fowler, Bud Cauley and Kurt Kitayama were among those who fell out of the top 30, with Ryan Fox claiming the final automatic spot.

Attention now turns to East Lake in Atlanta, where the top 30 in the FedExCup standings tee off next week in the Tour Championship — the last event of the playoffs and the one that decides the season's biggest prize.

foundayo-oral-glp1-uk-launch.headline: New once-daily diabetes and weight-loss pill Foundayo launches in UK pharmacies
foundayo-oral-glp1-uk-launch.body_md:
A once-daily pill that treats both type 2 diabetes and obesity went on sale in UK pharmacies today, the latest attempt by a drugmaker to prise the booming GLP-1 market away from the syringe. Orforglipron — sold under the brand name Foundayo — was cleared by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency on 10 August, and Eli Lilly says it is now reaching patients through private prescription and pharmacist-led supply services across the country.[^1]

The headline claim attached to the launch — that this is Europe's first oral GLP-1 pill — needs a footnote. It isn't quite right, and the distinction matters for anyone trying to work out who is actually winning this race.

## What the MHRA actually approved

Foundayo is licensed for two things: weight management in adults with a BMI of 30 or above (or 27–30 with a weight-related condition such as high blood pressure), and glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes, both alongside diet and exercise.[^2] Dosing starts at 0.8mg and climbs through five further steps to a maximum 36mg, with at least a month between increases — a slower, more forgiving escalation than some injectable regimens. Lilly's selling point is flexibility: the tablet can be taken at any time of day, with or without food or water, which is a genuine difference from Novo Nordisk's oral semaglutide, which requires an empty stomach and a 30-minute wait before eating.[^3]

Julian Beach, the MHRA's executive director of healthcare quality and access, said the agency was "pleased to be the first regulator in Europe to authorise this tablet for weight management and type 2 diabetes" — a carefully worded claim about *this molecule*, not about oral GLP-1s as a class.[^2]

That qualifier is doing real work. Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill — oral semaglutide, the same active ingredient as the injectable version — was approved by the MHRA on 11 June, two months before Foundayo, and had already reached UK pharmacies in stages through July and early August.[^4] So Britain's actual first oral GLP-1 was Danish, not American, and it beat Lilly to market by roughly six weeks. What Lilly has is the first authorisation of a structurally different drug: orforglipron is a small-molecule, non-peptide GLP-1 agonist, manufactured more like a conventional tablet and, Lilly argues, more cheaply at scale than peptide-based pills. Novo got there first; Lilly got there differently.

![Eli Lilly's corporate headquarters in Indianapolis, Indiana](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/05/Eli_Lilly_Corporate_Center%2C_Indianapolis%2C_Indiana%2C_USA.jpg)

## The efficacy trade-off

The clinical picture cuts in different directions depending on the indication, and it is worth being precise here rather than declaring a winner.

For weight loss, Novo's pill currently has the edge: in trial data, the high-dose Wegovy tablet produced average weight loss of 13.6–16.6% of body weight over roughly 64 weeks, against 12.4% for Foundayo's top 36mg dose over 72 weeks — a longer course for a smaller result.[^5] But in diabetes, the order reverses. In Lilly's own head-to-head ACHIEVE-3 trial, published in The Lancet, orforglipron's 36mg dose cut HbA1c by 2.2 percentage points and produced 9.2% weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes, against 1.4 points and 5.3% for oral semaglutide's top dose.[^6] Discontinuation due to side effects — mostly nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, the class-wide GLP-1 complaint — ran somewhat higher on orforglipron in that trial (8.7–9.7%) than on oral semaglutide (4.5–4.9%).[^6]

Neither drug is available on the NHS yet. Both require a separate assessment by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence before they can be prescribed for weight management on public funds; Lilly says Foundayo can already be used on the NHS for diabetes, but is seeking a NICE extension to cover obesity.[^1] Guidance on that question is expected in November.[^1] Until then, access runs through private prescription, at a cost — pharmacies are quoting Foundayo at roughly £129 to £179 a month, undercutting Wegovy's pill (£99–£269) and both companies' injectables, which run from around £140 to £375 depending on dose.[^7]

## A market that Lilly is not yet winning

The UK launch lands against an awkward backdrop for Lilly. Foundayo has been on sale in the United States since earlier this year, and its second-quarter sales there came in at $98m — slightly below analyst forecasts, and dwarfed by the roughly $500m Novo's oral Wegovy took in over the same three months.[^8] Citi analysts called the number "uninspiring."[^8] Lilly's response has been that this is a slow-build launch: its prescriber base nearly quadrupled from around 8,000 to 36,000 physicians during the quarter, a ramp its executives compare to the early trajectory of the injectable Zepbound before it became a blockbuster.[^8]

It is a curious inversion. Lilly dominates the injectable GLP-1 market — Mounjaro and Zepbound have consistently out-sold Novo's Ozempic and Wegovy shots on a head-to-head efficacy basis — yet in oral formulations, the company chasing convenience is currently the one playing catch-up. Some analysts still expect that to flip: Goldman Sachs has projected oral GLP-1s will make up around $22bn, or roughly a quarter, of the global weight-loss drug market by 2030, with Lilly's orforglipron eventually capturing the larger share of that pool.[^9] Whether that forecast holds will depend less on regulatory firsts than on something more mundane — pricing, prescriber comfort, and whether patients tolerate the tablet's side-effect profile well enough to stay on it.

## What's next

The UK's community pharmacies have already flagged one immediate concern: counterfeit and unlicensed GLP-1 products circulating online, a problem that predates Foundayo and is likely to intensify as demand for oral options grows.[^1] The nearer-term catalyst is regulatory rather than clinical — NICE's November verdict on whether Foundayo can be prescribed on the NHS for weight management will do more to determine its real UK market size than anything in this week's pharmacy launch. Lilly's next quarterly results, in the autumn, will show whether the US prescriber ramp is translating into the sales growth the company is promising.

norris-dutch-gp-title-fight.headline: Norris wins dramatic Dutch GP, revives F1 title fight after Verstappen crash
norris-dutch-gp-title-fight.body_md:
Lando Norris has a habit, this August, of being the last man standing when it matters. At Zandvoort on Sunday he did it again — hunting down Kimi Antonelli in the closing laps of a Dutch Grand Prix that started in the wet, restarted after a red flag, and ended with the sport's presumptive champion looking, for the first time all summer, beatable.

Norris won by 11.5 seconds in the end, a gap that flatters the calm of it. Getting there took a red-flagged opening lap, a standing restart, two virtual safety cars and a pass on both Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton on the same lap. It was Norris's second win in a row after Hungary, his thirteenth in Formula 1, and it cuts what had looked like a comfortable Antonelli procession down to something resembling a fight.

## A home race that lasted one corner

The day's first and most brutal story belonged to Max Verstappen. Starting on a damp track at the circuit he has turned into something close to a home fortress, the Dutchman got through Turn 1 and out onto the banked final corner before his rear end let go — a wheel clipping the painted line on the wet surface as he got back on the throttle, pitching the Red Bull into the outside wall hard enough to scatter debris across the track and end his race before it had properly begun.

![Max Verstappen on the podium at Zandvoort](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/2024-08-25_Motorsport%2C_Formel_1%2C_Gro%C3%9Fer_Preis_der_Niederlande_2024_STP_3973_by_Stepro_%28medium_crop%29.jpg)

Red Bull checked the car afterwards and found no mechanical fault. Verstappen, walking away unhurt, didn't look for excuses. "This weekend, of course, was disappointing," he said. "Disappointing pace, and a disappointing end to the weekend — I think you can sum it up like that." He added, with the flat practicality that has become his trademark even in defeat, that hitting the barrier head-on had actually hurt less than some of his previous crashes: "Everything's okay."

It was also, fittingly or not, the last Dutch Grand Prix on the calendar for now — Zandvoort's contract runs out after this year — which gave Verstappen's exit an extra sting for the crowd that had turned the dunes orange one final time.

## Norris grinds down the points leader

The red flag forced a standing restart on lap five, and it was Antonelli, not Norris, who got the better launch — diving past the McLaren into Turn 1 to take a lead he then stretched past a second. For the next several laps it looked like business as usual for the championship leader: quick out of trouble, comfortable under pressure, doing exactly what a driver 59 points clear is supposed to do.

![Kimi Antonelli at a 2025 grand prix weekend](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Kimi_Antonelli_at_the_2025_US_Grand_Prix_in_Austin%2C_TX_%28cropped%29.jpg)

What turned it was tyre strategy. Norris ran his middle stint seven laps longer than Antonelli's, banking fresher rubber for the run to the flag while the Mercedes' pace fell away. On lap 54 he used it — passing both Antonelli and Hamilton in the same move to retake a lead he would not give up again, then managing two further virtual-safety-car restarts without alarm. "Probably one of my better wins," Norris said afterwards. "We had to fight for it well but the pace was strong. We managed things incredibly well today."

Antonelli held on for second ahead of teammate George Russell, who was told to let his younger teammate through late on — a call Russell later defended as fair given Antonelli's tyre advantage in the moment, even as it left the two Mercedes drivers level on points in the championship, split only by countback. Antonelli, for his part, was candid about the deficit: strong starts had "saved" an otherwise uneasy weekend, he said, in which he lacked confidence in the car through the middle stints — the exact window Norris exploited.

## The title fight, recalculated

The numbers still favour Antonelli comfortably: he leads on 242 points to Norris's 159, an 83-point gap that no single race weekend closes. But the shape of the season has changed. A month ago this was a coronation in progress. Now it is a story with two winners in the last two races both wearing McLaren overalls, a Red Bull title threat that keeps crashing out of its own home race, and a Mercedes leader who is starting to sound less certain than his points total suggests.

Hamilton, fourth on the day, remains level with Russell on points but behind on wins — a reminder that Ferrari's title interest, while quieter than the front two storylines, hasn't gone away either.

What happens next depends on whether Norris's Zandvoort recovery was a one-off born of an unusually chaotic afternoon, or the start of a pattern. The next round will tell: if McLaren's tyre management held up under red flags and standing restarts, it should hold up in cleaner conditions too — and an 83-point gap has a way of looking smaller with ten races still to run than it does the day after a crash-strewn Sunday.

ceferin-infantino-uefa-fifa.headline: Infantino must remember he is European, says UEFA's Ceferin
ceferin-infantino-uefa-fifa.body_md:
Aleksander Ceferin does not do subtlety when he is angry, and this week he was angry. Asked on the Rest Is Politics podcast about Gianni Infantino's handling of FIFA, the UEFA president delivered the kind of line that ends up in headlines rather than committee minutes: someone, he said, should remind the FIFA boss that he is European — and that he seems to have forgotten it.

> "I think someone should remind him that he is a European, and that he was supported by UEFA, which he forgot."

It is a pointed jab, not a throwaway one. Infantino spent sixteen years working at UEFA's Nyon headquarters, nine of them as general secretary, before UEFA's own backing helped carry him into the FIFA presidency in 2016. Ceferin's implication is that Infantino has spent the years since acting as though that debt never existed.

![Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA president, pictured in 2019](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fa/2019_Aleksander_%C4%8Ceferin_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## What actually broke

The proximate cause is FIFA Forward Enterprise, a proposed vehicle through which FIFA would have sold a 21% stake in the commercial and ticketing rights to its competitions — including the World Cup — to a private investment company. UEFA says it learned of the plan through the media, with Ceferin finding out while on holiday. European federations voted to boycott FIFA competitions unless the scheme was dropped, and it duly was, in what UEFA officials have gleefully called Infantino's "humiliating climbdown" earlier this month.

Ceferin has not been shy about the comparison he reaches for. He has called FFE "even worse than the Super League" — a notable line from the man who spent 2021 leading football's establishment against that breakaway project, since the Super League was at least franchised chaos dressed up as ambition, whereas FFE, in his framing, was the outright sale of something that "belongs to everyone."

The dispute has since widened well past private equity. FIFA's decision to suspend Folarin Balogun's red-card ban during this summer's World Cup — clearing him to play the United States' last-16 tie against Belgium — drew accusations that Infantino had bent the rules after a phone call from Donald Trump. Ceferin skipped the final between Spain and Argentina in protest, calling Trump's intervention "more than shocking" and adding: "We have rules, and if you don't respect your own rules, then the game doesn't make any sense."

## The numbers turning against him

What began as institutional friction is curdling into something closer to a leadership crisis. The English and Welsh federations have both withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino's re-election, joined by Serbia, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland. UEFA itself has formally said it has lost confidence in him. Ceferin, for his part, insists he has no interest in running against Infantino himself — but he has said publicly that Infantino should either resign or face a contested vote at the FIFA Congress in Rabat next March.

## What's next

The next flashpoint is the 77th FIFA Congress, scheduled for 18 March 2027 in Morocco, where Infantino's re-election was expected to be a formality before this summer unravelled that assumption. Whether a credible challenger emerges — and whether more federations follow England and Wales in withdrawing support — will determine if Ceferin's rhetoric translates into an actual contest, or simply into eighteen months of the sport's two most powerful men trading insults in public.

oneill-devolution-backing.headline: Jim O'Neill rules out government role but backs Burnham's devolution agenda
oneill-devolution-backing.body_md:
Jim O'Neill has spent four decades telling other people how economies should be run — as Goldman Sachs' chief economist, as the man who coined BRIC, as a Conservative Treasury minister under David Cameron. So there was a certain shape to the story when word went round Westminster that Andy Burnham wanted him back in government, this time as chief economic adviser. And there was a certain shape, too, to O'Neill turning it down.

> "I've decided to not take a formal role," O'Neill said, adding that it wasn't down to any rift with the prime minister over policy.

The sticking point, by his own account, was duller than intrigue: a blind trust. Taking an official post would have meant handing control of his business interests to a trustee for the duration, the standard price of ministerial propriety. O'Neill, who chairs several private ventures and still sits on assorted boards, wasn't willing to pay it. "I don't want the constraints of a blind trust and all the constraints that would be necessary," he said — adding, with the air of a man who has done this job once already and doesn't miss the paperwork, that he was enjoying his current arrangements "too much."

![Jim O'Neill, Baron O'Neill of Gatley](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Official_portrait_of_Lord_O%27Neill_of_Gatley_crop_2.jpg/250px-Official_portrait_of_Lord_O%27Neill_of_Gatley_crop_2.jpg)

## Backing the policy, not the payroll

What makes the episode worth a second look is what O'Neill said next. Devolution — the transfer of fiscal and planning power away from Whitehall to city-region mayors — is the policy Burnham has staked his premiership on, and O'Neill is unambiguously for it.

> "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else," he said, offering instead to "be a voice if they want to talk to me — that is, occasionally."

That's not a small endorsement. O'Neill has been arguing for fiscal devolution to England's cities since long before Burnham held any office at all — his 2014 review for George Osborne, "Fixing the Foundations," helped lay the intellectual groundwork for the Northern Powerhouse. He chairs the advisory board of the Greater Manchester Local Enterprise Partnership and grew up in Gatley, a few miles from the mayoral office Burnham once ran before Downing Street. If anyone in British public life has skin in this particular game, it's him.

Which is what makes the abstention notable rather than merely procedural. O'Neill isn't withholding support for the devolution agenda — he's withholding his name from the government executing it, on terms that have nothing to do with the policy itself and everything to do with the personal cost of formal office. Read generously, that's a seasoned operator choosing influence over title, preferring to needle a government he broadly likes from outside its structures than be bound inside them. Read less generously, it's a reminder that persuading a well-regarded economist to say nice things about your flagship policy is a lower bar than persuading him to bet his own arrangements on delivering it.

Either way, Burnham gets the quote without the appointment, and O'Neill gets to keep saying, as he has said in one form or another since 2001, that Britain's cities are underpowered — without having to answer for whether Downing Street actually fixes that.

The next marker will be the government's devolution white paper, expected to set out how much fiscal latitude mayors actually get. O'Neill's applause from the sidelines will only mean as much as what's in it.

china-cabbage-formaldehyde-probe.headline: China probes wholesaler for using formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
china-cabbage-formaldehyde-probe.body_md:
The video runs less than a minute. A worker in Kangbao county, in China's northern Hebei province, lifts cabbage after cabbage by the stem and dips the root end into a basin of clear liquid before stacking it onto a freight truck. Off to one side sits a plastic container labelled, in Chinese, "formaldehyde solution." A local blogger posted the clip on August 22; within a day, Hebei authorities had confirmed it was real.

By August 23, police in Kangbao had detained the individuals involved and impounded the vehicles used to move the treated produce, according to [Global Times](https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202608/1368800.shtml). Random sampling of the batches in question came back positive for formaldehyde. China's State Council Food Safety Commission, the Ministry of Agriculture and the market regulation authority have since ordered a nationwide inspection sweep of vegetable wholesalers, with local officials told to trace the cabbages' distribution routes and stop any that had not yet reached consumers. State media commentary was blunt: the wholesalers, People's Daily wrote, had "crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."

Formaldehyde is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, with established links to nasopharyngeal cancer and leukaemia in humans. Dipping cabbage stems in a dilute solution is thought to slow the rot that sets in during long, unrefrigerated truck journeys — buying growers and traders an extra two or three days of shelf life on stock that would otherwise spoil in transit.

![A cart loaded with napa cabbages in Inner Mongolia, China](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2b/Truck_of_dabaicai_in_Lindong.jpg)

## A familiar shortcut

The practice is not new, and that is precisely the problem. In 2012, Xinhua reporters found wholesalers in Qingzhou, Shandong province, spraying cabbages with formaldehyde as a matter of routine, a habit that had reportedly persisted for at least three years beforehand. The underlying economics have not changed since: China's fragmented vegetable logistics chain still runs heavily on non-refrigerated trucks, which few small wholesalers can afford to swap for cold-chain equivalents. Cabbage stacked tightly in an open truck bed can turn within two to three days: fast enough to wipe out a trader's margin, slow enough that a cheap chemical fix looks worth the risk.

That gap between what the rules require and what the transport network can actually deliver is the structural part of the story. Beijing has run repeated crackdowns on food-safety violations since the 2008 melamine-tainted milk scandal, and periodic sweeps have caught everything from banned growth promoters in pork to industrial dye in spices. Each episode produces detentions, inspection orders and pledges to fix the system. Each recurrence suggests the incentives underneath it, thin margins, poor cold-chain coverage, patchy enforcement at the wholesale level, remain largely intact.

## Why traders should care

China is not a marginal player in the vegetable trade it is now investigating. Japan sources roughly 94% of its cabbage and brassica imports from China, making that single supply corridor close to irreplaceable for year-round retail stability. South Korea and other regional buyers lean on Chinese produce in similar, if less extreme, proportions. A confirmed adulteration case, even one confined so far to a single county, tends to trigger heightened border sampling in importing markets long before any government formally tightens quarantine rules: customs agencies default to caution once a contamination method has been publicly verified.

It is not yet known whether any of the treated Kangbao cabbage reached export channels; Chinese authorities say that tracing is still underway. But agricultural commodity desks watching Chinese produce flows have reason to treat this as more than a local food-safety item. Recurring adulteration scandals erode the credibility of routine testing regimes, and testing credibility is the thing that keeps vegetable shipments moving across borders without added friction.

## What to watch

The near-term marker is whether Beijing's nationwide inspection order turns up further cases beyond Kangbao, which would confirm this as a wider practice rather than an isolated lapse, as was the case in 2012. Beyond that, any statement from Japanese or South Korean quarantine authorities on stepped-up sampling of Chinese vegetable imports would be the first sign the episode is spilling into trade friction rather than staying a domestic regulatory story.

mayors-planning-override-powers.headline: England mayors to get powers to overrule councils on major planning decisions
mayors-planning-override-powers.body_md:
Thirteen English mayors are about to acquire a power London has had for a quarter of a century: the right to overrule the town hall next door.

Under plans confirmed this week, regional mayors — from Greater Manchester and Liverpool City Region to the West Midlands and West of England — will be able to "call in" major planning applications, taking decisions out of council hands entirely and directing them to be approved or refused. It mirrors the authority the London mayor has held since 2000, when Ken Livingstone was first handed the ability to step over borough councils on schemes of citywide significance.

The thresholds are specific rather than sweeping: developments of more than 150 homes, commercial schemes over 15,000 square metres, or any building taller than 30 metres — roughly ten storeys and up. Mayors are also expected to gain the power to grant "up-front permission" on some sites, letting building start without a developer filing an individual application at all.

![Cranes over the Manchester skyline](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Cranes_over_the_Manchester_Skyline%2C_geograph_5726997_by_Anthony_Parkes.jpg/1280px-Cranes_over_the_Manchester_Skyline%2C_geograph_5726997_by_Anthony_Parkes.jpg)

## A pitch built on frustration with delay

The case for the change is essentially about friction. Councils can sit on large applications for months, sometimes years, weighing objections from residents, ward councillors and conservation groups — a process defenders call democratic accountability and critics call gridlock. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook framed the new powers as "an essential part of the toolkit" mayors need to deliver homes and regeneration, language that fits neatly into the government's target of 1.5 million new homes in England this Parliament, a goal it is visibly behind on.

Ten of the fourteen devolved mayors have already backed the move — a notable show of unity for a policy that, on its face, hands them power at councils' expense. A consultation is due to be published in the coming days, which is where the sharper edges of implementation — appeal rights, ministerial oversight, exactly how "significance" gets defined case by case — will get worked out.

## The pushback

Not everyone is convinced concentrating authority is the fix. Shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly argued the government was "stripping councils . . . of their ability to make planning decisions in their own communities", the traditional Conservative line that local control should mean local control, full stop.

The government's rebuttal is that call-in powers are a backstop, not a takeover. Councils keep the vast majority of applications; ministers retain their own intervention rights; and any call-in decision still has to comply with local plans and national policy — mayors cannot simply wave through whatever they like. The pitch is less "mayors decide everything" and more "mayors get to break the specific logjams that stall the biggest schemes."

## What it doesn't fix

The more interesting caveat is the one nobody in the debate disputes: planning approval is only one bottleneck among several. Material costs, labour shortages and financing conditions all constrain how much actually gets built once permission is granted — a call-in power does nothing to a brick shortage or a stretched contractor. Recent delivery figures cited alongside the announcement — Salford running well ahead of its housing target, Leeds and Knowsley outperforming theirs too — suggest some mayoral areas are already building at pace under existing rules, which cuts both ways: it is evidence the tool can work, and evidence that a permission problem was never the whole story everywhere.

Watch for the consultation itself, expected within days, for the fine print on how call-ins interact with existing local plans — and for whether opposition councils treat this as a fight worth having or a power they quietly welcome the next time a scheme stalls on their own doorstep.

robot-horse-china-conference.headline: Robot horse and rider steal the show at Chinese robotics conference
robot-horse-china-conference.body_md:
The horse walked in mechanical, deliberate steps across the exhibition floor in Beijing, a humanoid robot in the saddle, reins in its metal hands. It was not a stunt cooked up for a keynote — it was a product demo. The four-legged machine underneath, called the Qiji X1, is built by a Beijing startup named DaxAI Robotics, and as of this month you can buy one for 289,000 yuan, or about $43,000.

The scene, staged at the 2026 World Robot Conference, which opened in Beijing on 19 August and runs through the weekend, was the standout image from a five-day event drawing a record 300-plus exhibitors and, organisers say, 271,000 in-person visitors. It also happened to be exactly the kind of story that travels well and explains almost nothing: a robot horse is a better photograph than a balance sheet.

## What the machine actually does

Strip away the novelty and the Qiji X1 is a load-carrying quadruped with a saddle bolted on. DaxAI, founded around 2025 by Wang Kun, a veteran of autonomous-driving and robotics work, says the X1 carries up to 300 kilograms at roughly 10 km/h, with a range of about 40 kilometres, and is built to cross gravel, mud and steep slopes that would stop a wheeled vehicle. A wheel-legged sibling, the XS, sells for 359,000 yuan (about $53,000). DaxAI pitches both for off-road haulage and emergency-rescue logistics — getting supplies, or people, over terrain a truck can't reach — rather than for anyone's daily commute. Even boosters describe the riding motion as noticeably stiff next to a real horse, which is the honest way to put it: this is a proof of concept with a price tag, not a finished consumer product.

The robot horse shared the spotlight with a related event a few days later, the World Humanoid Robot Games, where a humanoid perched on a similar mount drew a bow and released an arrow at the opening ceremony — closer to circus act than industrial showcase, and a reminder that this particular week in Beijing was built for spectacle as much as substance.

## The context that actually moves money

The conference itself is not nothing: China says its humanoid makers shipped 90% of the world's units last year across more than 330 models, with first-quarter 2026 exports up 210% year-on-year. But the number that mattered to investors landed a few days before the horse did, when Unitree Robotics — the quadruped and humanoid maker best known for backflipping robot dogs — priced its Shanghai listing at 150.8 yuan a share, valuing the company near $9bn, and then surged as much as 629% on its trading debut. That is capital markets pricing in a robotics bet with real revenue behind it: Unitree reported 1.7bn yuan in 2025 sales and has delivered some 18,000 units. DaxAI, by contrast, has disclosed no funding round, no production numbers beyond the sticker price, and no filing of any kind.

## What to watch

None of that makes the horse worthless as a signal — China's robotics sector is visibly scaling, and DaxAI's list price suggests it expects buyers beyond hobbyists, plausibly logistics or disaster-response agencies drawn by the terrain claims. But a demo lap around a convention hall is not a purchase order. The event to actually watch is Unitree's post-IPO run as the first humanoid-robot maker listed in mainland China, since its share price will now serve as the market's real-time verdict on how much of this industry's promise investors are willing to pay for today. The World Robot Conference closes this weekend; whether DaxAI ever discloses a funding round or a customer name is the next test of whether the horse is a business or just good theatre.

disraeli-photo-missing-artworks.headline: Photo of Disraeli among missing parliamentary artworks, FoI request reveals
disraeli-photo-missing-artworks.body_md:
Somewhere in the vast, cluttered inventory of the Palace of Westminster, a photograph of Benjamin Disraeli has gone astray. So has an engraving of William Wilberforce, a satirical cartoon of Barbara Castle drawn as Florence Nightingale, and a photograph of Margaret Beckett, Britain's first female foreign secretary. In total, more than 65 works from Parliament's own art collection cannot currently be located — a fact that only came to light because someone thought to ask.

The figures emerged from a Freedom of Information request submitted by the Press Association, which asked Parliament to account for its holdings since the start of 2024. The Disraeli photograph, taken by the prolific Victorian portraitist John Jabez Edwin Mayall — who also sat Queen Victoria, Charles Dickens and Karl Marx in front of his camera — is the most eye-catching name on the list, but hardly the only one of note. The missing Wilberforce piece is a 19th-century engraving by William Holl; there is also a cartoon by Isaac Cruikshank and, more recently, a Martin Rowson cartoon from 1995 depicting John Major lancing the "boil" of that year's Conservative leadership challenge.

![Portrait of Benjamin Disraeli, National Portrait Gallery](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/89/Benjamin-Disraeli-Earl-of-Beaconsfield_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A working collection, not a vault

Parliament's response to the disclosure was measured rather than alarmed. A spokesperson said there was "little evidence of works of art going permanently missing from the Parliamentary Art Collection," pointing out that the roughly 8,500-piece collection — split between the Commons and the Lords, and covering everything from oil paintings to coins and wallpaper — is a working one. Pieces are moved between offices, committee rooms and storage on a rolling basis, get mislaid in the shuffle, and often turn up again: five of the works reported missing this year have already been found. None, Parliament insists, has been formally written off or booked as a financial loss.

That explanation has some historical cover. A near-identical FoI request in 2018 turned up 224 unaccounted-for works, including portraits of William Pitt the Younger and a wartime painting by William John MacLeod depicting the aftermath of the bombing of Parliament. Most of those, eventually, resurfaced too. Set against that precedent, this year's total of 65-odd looks less like a fresh scandal than a recurring administrative quirk of running an active museum spread across a working legislature.

## Why the gap still matters

Still, the pattern is worth pausing on. An institution that catalogues its own history as carefully as Parliament does — the Speaker's Advisory Committee on Works of Art has overseen the collection since 1841 — is nonetheless unable, at any given moment, to say with certainty where every item in it sits. That is not evidence of theft or negligence so much as a reminder that inventory control is hard even for bodies whose entire self-image rests on institutional memory. A Georgian engraving stored in the wrong archive box carries no financial consequence for Parliament. The habits of mind that let it go missing, though, are the same ones that show up in less forgivable places when the assets being tracked are documents, contracts or public money rather than portraits.

What happens next is mostly a matter of patience. Parliament says its art teams periodically audit and relocate works as offices change hands, so a further round of "discoveries" — as happened with five pieces already this year — is the likeliest outcome, rather than any formal loss report. The next test of how seriously the gap is being taken will be whether a subsequent FoI request, whenever one is filed, shows the list shrinking or simply refreshing itself with new names.
